[body] Example 10: Walking cadence
[body] In the article “Can We Really Walk Straight?” (Amer. J. of Physical Anthropology, 1992: 19–27) reported on an experiment in which each of 20 healthy men was asked to walk as straight as possible to a target 60m away at normal speed.
[body] Consider the following observations on cadence (number of strides per second):
[body] .95 .85 .92 .95 .93 .86 1.00 .92 .85 .81 .78 .93 .93 1.05 .93 1.06 .96 .81 .96
[body] Summarize the data; interpret and discuss.
[body] Prof. Oke (UMass Amherst) CEE 260/MIE 273 M1b: Summarizing Data September 10, 2026 15 / 16

novice.takeaway: The slide asks us to summarize and interpret 19 measured walking-cadence values from an experiment involving 20 healthy men walking toward a target.
questions: Why are there 19 observations for 20 men?
What does walking straight have to do with cadence?
novice.inferred_claim: Use summary statistics and plots to describe these walking-cadence measurements.

peer.takeaway: The slide gives 19 measured walking cadences from a straight-walking experiment and asks us to summarize their center, spread, and distribution in strides per second.
questions: Why does the text say 20 men but list 19 observations?
peer.inferred_claim: Use descriptive summaries to characterize the walking-cadence measurements.

expert.takeaway: The slide asks us to summarize and interpret 19 reported walking-cadence measurements, in strides per second, from an experiment involving 20 healthy men walking toward a 60 m target.
questions: Why are only 19 cadence observations shown for 20 men?
expert.inferred_claim: Use descriptive statistics and distribution summaries to characterize the walking-cadence data.
